headline: Cold northwest flow brings scattered Kentucky showers and a few possible flakes; the Upstate stays dry as a hard weekend freeze develops
disclaimer: Independent amateur analysis. This is not an official forecast or warning. Follow the National Weather Service and local authorities during hazardous weather.

refresh.workflow: Update and commit forecast.json once. GitHub Actions automatically locks the prior issue in forecast-history.json. Then verify the GitHub Pages URL; every Google Sites embed reads the same file and refreshes automatically.

kentucky.name: Central Kentucky
kentucky.subtitle: Danville primary · Lexington comparison
kentucky.summary: Central Kentucky is behind the cold front and remains beneath a deep eastern trough. Gusty northwest flow, wraparound moisture and passing shortwaves support scattered light showers today and Friday. A shower may briefly mix with snow late tonight through Friday evening, but no accumulation is forecast around Danville or Lexington. High pressure then clears the sky Saturday and sets up a widespread hard freeze Saturday night.
kentucky.currentConditions: At 7:15 AM EST, KDVK reported 45°F with a 43°F dew point, northwest wind near 7 mph, visibility above 10 miles, scattered clouds at 1,500 feet and an overcast layer at 6,500 feet. At 6:54 AM, KLEX reported 46°F with a 42°F dew point, northwest wind near 13 mph, 10-mile visibility and an overcast 7,000-foot ceiling. No official NWS point alert was active for Danville at the final issuance check.

days.label: Thursday / Thursday night
days.hazard: OFFICIAL NWS ALERT STATUS: no active point alert covers Danville at issuance. Independent concerns are blustery northwest wind and brief light showers. A few flakes could mix with a shower late tonight, but no accumulation or travel impact is expected.
days.forecast: Broken low clouds and occasional brighter intervals continue as northwest wind increases to 10–15 mph with gusts of 20–30 mph. The most-likely Danville high is near 53°F. Shortwave energy and shallow wraparound moisture favor brief showers mainly from noon to about 10 PM, with a second low-probability window overnight. Most locations receive only a trace to about 0.08 inch. The most-likely Friday-morning low is near 37°F. Thunder, heavy rain and dense fog are not expected.

days.label: Friday / Friday night
days.precipitation: 35–45% light showers; 25–35% chance of flakes or a brief mix
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert covers Friday at issuance. Independent concerns are winterlike wind chills, a widespread freeze Friday night and brief rain or snow showers. Warm ground and light precipitation strongly favor no accumulation around Danville or Lexington.
days.forecast: Cyclonic northwest flow keeps Friday mostly cloudy and winterlike. Intermittent light showers are possible during the morning and again from early afternoon into the evening as another impulse rotates through the trough. The most-likely Danville high is near 43°F. Northwest wind runs 7–12 mph with gusts of 15–24 mph. A shower can briefly mix with or change to snow, especially toward evening, but measurable accumulation is not forecast. Clearing later Friday night supports a most-likely Saturday-morning low near 28°F, with colder rural valleys in the middle 20s.

days.label: Saturday / early Sunday
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert covers Saturday at issuance. Independent concern is a hard freeze Saturday night into Sunday morning. Snow, rain, thunder and advisory-level wind are not forecast after any early stray flurry ends.
days.forecast: Any early stray flurry ends, then high pressure brings partial clearing followed by mostly sunny, dry weather. The most-likely Danville high is near 46°F. Northwest wind eases to 3–8 mph with gusts around 10–18 mph. Clear sky and light wind Saturday night promote strong radiational cooling. The most-likely early-Sunday low is near 25°F, with sheltered valleys capable of 21–23°F.

kentucky.bottomLine: Danville remains blustery and cold behind the front. Brief showers are possible today and Friday, and a shower may contain a few flakes late tonight or Friday without accumulation. Most-likely temperatures are 53/37°F today and tonight, 43/28°F Friday and Friday night, and 46/25°F Saturday and Saturday night. Saturday turns dry, followed by a hard freeze.
kentucky.confidence: High on the cold regime, Saturday drying and weekend freeze; moderate-high on temperatures and wind; moderate on the placement of brief showers; moderate-low on whether Danville actually observes flakes

upstate.name: Upstate South Carolina
upstate.subtitle: Clemson primary · Central/Pickens County comparison
upstate.summary: The cold front crosses the Clemson–Central corridor dry this morning, apart from a localized early low-cloud or sprinkle pocket near Central. Mixing quickly clears the shallow moisture and produces gusty west to northwest wind. The corridor then stays sunny and dry beneath the eastern trough Friday and high pressure Saturday. Freezing temperatures become increasingly likely Friday night and widespread Saturday night, especially around Central and sheltered Pickens County terrain.
upstate.currentConditions: At 6:54 AM EST, KCEU reported 54°F with a 52°F dew point, west-southwest wind near 10 mph with a gust near 20 mph, clear sky and unrestricted visibility. At 7:35 AM, KLQK reported 52°F with a 50°F dew point, north wind near 3 mph, 7-mile visibility and only scattered clouds at 300 feet after the earlier shallow ceiling and 0.01 inch of rain. KAND and KGSP were clear at 6:56 and 6:53 AM. No official NWS point alert was active for Clemson or Central at the final issuance check. Tempest data was not used.

days.label: Thursday / Thursday night
days.precipitation: 10% or less early; 5% or less thereafter
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert is active for Clemson or Central. Independent concern is a gusty dry frontal passage. Wind Advisory criteria are not expected in the corridor, and freezing temperatures should be isolated to the coldest hollows late tonight.
days.forecast: A localized low cloud or stray sprinkle around Central ends early as mixing deepens; the corridor then turns sunny and dry. Most-likely highs are near 66°F at KCEU and 65°F at KLQK. West to west-northwest wind increases to 10–16 mph with gusts of 22–30 mph, then eases after sunset. Most-likely Friday-morning lows are near 41°F at KCEU and 36°F at KLQK. Thunder and widespread fog are not expected.

days.label: Friday / Friday night
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert is active. Independent concern is a Friday-night freeze, greatest around KLQK and sheltered terrain. GSP ended seasonal freeze products on November 11, so the absence of a Freeze Warning does not mean there is no freeze risk.
days.forecast: Sunny, dry and distinctly cooler conditions continue beneath the deep eastern trough. Most-likely highs are near 58°F at KCEU and 57°F at KLQK. West-northwest wind runs 5–12 mph with gusts of 16–24 mph and diminishes overnight. Most-likely Saturday-morning lows are near 35°F at KCEU and 30°F at KLQK. The regional freeze probability is about 65%, focused on Central, rural Pickens County and sheltered hollows.

days.label: Saturday / early Sunday
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert is active. Independent concern is a widespread freeze Saturday night into Sunday morning, with hard-freeze readings possible in colder hollows. Seasonal freeze products have ended; rain, snow, thunder and advisory-level wind are not forecast in the corridor.
days.forecast: Sunny and dry conditions continue as surface high pressure settles closer to the region. Most-likely highs are near 56°F at KCEU and 55°F at KLQK. Northwest wind of 2–7 mph with gusts around 8–16 mph becomes light Saturday night. Clear sky, exceptionally low moisture and calm conditions support most-likely early-Sunday lows near 33°F at KCEU and 27°F at KLQK; colder hollows may reach the middle 20s. The regional freeze probability is about 90%.

upstate.bottomLine: The Clemson–Central corridor turns sunny and gusty after any early low cloud or stray sprinkle near Central. The forecast then stays dry. Most-likely station values are KCEU 66/41°F, 58/35°F and 56/33°F and KLQK 65/36°F, 57/30°F and 55/27°F. Freeze risk rises from localized late tonight to about 65% Friday night and 90% Saturday night.
upstate.confidence: High on the dry post-frontal pattern and Thursday gusts; moderate-high on daytime temperatures and Friday-night freeze; moderate on exact station lows and Saturday cold magnitude

analysisLinks.label: College of DuPage satellite and radar

sourceNotes: OFFICIAL ALERTS: no active NWS point alert was present for Danville, Clemson or Central at the final issuance check. Official alerts remain explicitly separate from national outlooks and this independent analysis.

The 11:17Z Louisville discussion places Kentucky behind the front beneath a deep Great Lakes/eastern trough. Wraparound moisture, steep low-level lapse rates and passing shortwaves support scattered light showers today and Friday, northwest gusts around 20–30 mph today, and a low chance of Bluegrass flakes. Warm ground prevents accumulation. High pressure brings widespread subfreezing temperatures this weekend.

Chris Bailey’s exact November 12 Kentucky Weather Center post and readable First Flakes map were consulted as accepted authoritative source material. Bailey supports showers today, rain and snow showers or flurries Friday into Friday night, upper-30s/lower-40s highs over central/eastern Kentucky Friday, weekend highs mainly in the 40s and lows in the lower/middle 20s. His map places Danville in ‘a few flakes possible’ and confines light accumulation potential to southeastern high mountains. Details absent or unreadable were left unknown.

The 11:32Z Greenville-Spartanburg discussion supports a dry cold-frontal passage in the Clemson–Central corridor, gusty wind below advisory criteria, and the coldest air of the season. Northwest-flow snow remains confined to the higher NC/TN border terrain. Freeze products ended with the growing season on November 11, so the lack of a warning is not evidence against the independent Friday- and Saturday-night freeze risk.

Official point forecasts support Danville near 53/36°F, 45/27°F and 46/24°F; Clemson near 66/39°F, 58/33°F and 56/31°F; and Central near 66/38°F, 57/32°F and 56/30°F. The independent cards retain these centers inside the empirically calibrated regional widths and apply maintained station corrections in the prose.

Current observations showed post-frontal low cloud and northwest wind at KDVK/KLEX. KCEU, KAND and KGSP were clear, while KLQK alone had a shallow 300-foot ceiling and 0.01 inch of recent rain. That localized early moisture is acknowledged, but the radar, surrounding observations and all post-frontal guidance support rapid drying. Tempest was excluded.

College of DuPage radar at 12:05–12:10Z showed no organized heavy precipitation over either forecast corridor. Infrared imagery showed the wraparound Kentucky cloud shield, and the 12Z surface analysis placed both regions behind or along the departing front. The 00Z 500-mb, 850-mb moisture and precipitable-water analyses support a deep eastern trough and progressive drying.

Every currently visible COD family was inspected: HRRR, RAP, RRFS, GEM-RDPS, GEM-GDPS, ECMWF, GFS, AIFS, AIGFS, CFSv2, GEFS, REFS, AIFS-ENS and AIGEFS. Temperature, pressure, wind, 500-mb, 850-mb, moisture, cloud, precipitation, CAPE and ensemble fields were reviewed as available. All families support the eastern trough, strong cold advection, near-zero inland instability and 1024–1030-mb weekend high pressure.

COD’s short-range HRRR, RAP, RRFS and REFS show transient trace/light wraparound precipitation across central/eastern Kentucky; the globals and AI families range from trace to light. The blended forecast therefore uses scattered-shower probabilities and very light totals rather than calling Kentucky completely dry or predicting steady rain. Clemson remains dry or trace-level across the model set.

Weekend cold magnitude is the main model disagreement. RRFS, Canadian and AI guidance lean colder, while GFS and ECMWF are somewhat milder. GEFS, AIFS-ENS and AIGEFS agree strongly on the cold regime, with spread mainly in amplitude. Official point guidance, fresh BUFKIT profiles, NBM, station corrections and calibrated widths resolve the local values without giving unverified AI or coarse families artificial weights.
